The Plan

How to read The Plan

Two price lines and one demand line. Our forecast is what we expected each hour to cost, and it is the projection the plan below was solved against — it runs the width of the frame, and past where the plan stops being committed it is drawn broken. The settled price is the fifteen-minute real-time price at HB_SOUTH, this account’s hub, interval by interval as each one publishes; the newest interval carries a dot. ERCOT system demand (live) is the dotted line: how much power the whole ERCOT grid is using, read every five minutes, in gigawatts on the right-hand axis. It is market-wide, not a figure at this account’s hub, and it is not a price.

Everything left of the upright is a record. Each day’s pale line is the price that morning’s plan was solved against, archived and hashed at issue; the bars beneath are the blocks it scheduled, each labelled with its energy in MWh — the number alone on a block too short to hold the unit.

The settled price is at HB_SOUTH. The five-minute price row in The Prints below is different: it is ERCOT system-wide, not a price at this account’s hub, and it is never drawn here.

Right of the upright the planned line is drawn faint. From the last hour this record prices at or before that moment, the line is drawn faint. The changeover therefore lands on the upright line or to the left of it, never to its right — it snaps back to an hour the record actually prices rather than cutting the line at an instant between two of them.

Those are the same archived record’s prices, for hours that had not arrived when this screen was built: nothing in that stretch is a forecast made since the morning.

Past where the plan stops being committed, the forecast line continues drawn broken, and no scorecard is published on those hours.

The upright is now; the rule to its right is where the plan stops being committed. That rule sits twenty-four hours after the newest issue — the masthead names the issue it is measured from — and everything right of it is provisional: re-solved at the next issue, and never graded. The hatched bars beyond it are those blocks.

Each line is drawn at the resolution its record keeps: the forecast holds one price across each hour it prices, the settled price holds each settlement interval, and the demand line holds each five-minute reading until the next one. A line steps where a new value begins and never slopes between two of them, because nothing is known about the minutes in between.

Click anywhere on the graph to read what the record says about that moment; click again to clear it. The arrow keys walk it a quarter-hour at a time once the graph has focus, and Esc closes it.

− and + — − widens the window from 20 hours at the closest step out to 244 hours, one step per press — the box between the two buttons names the width at each step; + brings it back in. Time compresses as the window widens, so the same record draws a busier line — that is the record, not the drawing. Every step of the control draws the same values at the same resolution; nothing is averaged as the window widens. The blocks, the day names and the boundary marks keep their own edges at every step — they narrow with the clock rather than being redrawn.

The Prints

How to read The Prints

System-wide — ERCOT system-wide, not a price at HB_SOUTH, this account’s hub: the market’s own five-minute run, published about 5–10 minutes after each SCED run. It carries no congestion and nothing settles at it, so on a congested day it can sit far from the settled row beneath it, even on the other side of zero.

Settled — the settled hub price for a closed hour — it arrives after the hour ends, so the current hour is always blank here. It is why that row spans three columns while the row above it moves every one: the system-wide row prints every five minutes and the settled row every fifteen, after its interval closes. Two cadences, two quantities. We do not manufacture a five-minute settlement price out of the system-wide one; the gap between the two rows is real and it is shown.

− and + — one control for the whole scope of the graph. − always puts more time on the screen and + always puts less there at closer range; press either far enough and the step changes from widening the columns to widening the buckets, which is how the tape reaches back further than a day. A rolled-up price is a time-weighted average: past five minutes the system-wide row is averaged over the bucket, and past fifteen the settled row is too. A bucket shows a settled figure only when every fifteen-minute interval inside it has settled, and reads pending when they have not. Gaps are counted in five-minute intervals whatever the bucket, so no line is drawn across a hole. The box between the two buttons always names the bucket now on screen.
